dist.heading: Distance
dist.note: Worked from the chart’s own output. The difference in sun time is an angle at 15° to the hour. Taken with the two latitudes it gives the angle between the two places, and Gleason’s sixty geographical miles to the degree turns that into a distance. Haversine is used to verify the consistency of the time conversion to geographical miles. A straight ruler laid across the chart is not this, because a line that misses the centre is not on a radial.

note.recentred: The chart is recentred on A, so every straight line out of A is a radial and the ruler is exact along it. Distances between two other points on this view are not.
note.radial: This line passes through the centre of the chart, so it lies along a radial and the ruler is reading the scale it appears to be reading.
note.offCentre: This line does not pass through the centre, so it is not along a radial. Recentre the chart on A to measure it with a straight edge.
note.pole: One dot on a globe projection, one whole circle on this one. The dashed ring is the pole itself, stretched to the size this projection gives it. Every part of that ring is the pole. The marker is just a handle. It sits on the other point's meridian, so the line between them runs along a radial and measures correctly.

l1.title: Longitude into time
l1.body: Greenwich to New York. Read the difference of longitude, then take it at four minutes to the degree. This is the calculation the sheet was patented for.
l2.title: The radial is exact
l2.body: Pole to Singapore. The line runs straight out from the centre, so it lies along a radial and the ruler reads the scale correctly. Ruler and shortest distance agree exactly.
l3.title: The ruler off to one side
l3.body: Sydney to Santiago on the chart as printed. The straight line never comes near the centre, so it is not on a radial and the reading is far out.
l4.title: Recentre, and the ruler is true
l4.body: The same two places, the same engraving, replotted about Sydney. Now the line to Santiago is a radial, and the ruler reads correctly.
l5.title: Why recentring works
l5.body: The same Sydney to Santiago measurement, recentred. Read this one alongside the chart.
l5.d1: Equidistant is a real guarantee, but a narrow one. On this projection distances are true only along straight lines running outward from the centre. Nowhere else.
l5.d2: Gleason put the centre at the north pole. So a straight edge from the pole to anywhere reads correctly. So do any two places on one meridian, because that line passes through the centre on its way.
l5.d3: Sydney to Santiago never comes near the centre. That is why the ruler there overstates the distance by more than double.
l5.d4: Here is the part that does the work: the centre is not a property of the world. It is a choice made when the projection is drawn. Gleason chose the pole. Nothing stops you choosing Sydney.
l5.d5: Recentring takes the same engraving, the same ink, and asks where each piece of it lands if Sydney is the centre instead. Sydney is then in the middle, the line out to Santiago runs straight out from the centre, and the guarantee applies to it. The ruler reads 6,118 n.m., which is right.
l5.d6: The straight line started working because the one place the projection can be trusted was moved to the place being measured from. Nothing was corrected on the map.
l5.d7: The same limit still applies, one step along: this view is true from A only. Measure between two other points on it and you are reading a chord again.
l5.d8: None of this is a workaround. Polar route charts are recentred on the departure airport for exactly this reason, and the pivot at the centre of Gleason's own sheet is there because every operation his patent describes is an angular one taken about that point.
l6.title: A degree of longitude is not a fixed distance
l6.body: Cape Town and Sydney sit almost on the same parallel. A degree of longitude between them is still four minutes of sun time, the same as anywhere. It is not 60 miles. At 34 degrees south it is about 50. Gleason tabulates that shrinkage in his Fig. 43.
l7.title: One point, stretched into a circle
l7.body: North pole to south pole. Look at how B is drawn.
l7.d1: The projection keeps the north pole as a point. So A is a dot at the centre.
l7.d2: It does not keep the south pole as a point. It stretches it. So B is the dashed circle around the rim.
l7.d3: That circle is not a route to B. It is B.
l7.d4: One dot on a globe projection, one whole circle on this one. Same place, laid out two different ways.
l7.d5: Every projection has to open the surface up somewhere. This one keeps the north pole whole. The cost lands on the opposite point, and the south pole gets pulled out into the entire boundary. Nothing is hidden and nothing is invented. It is stretched.
l7.d6: Every part of that ring is the south pole. All of it, equally. The marker on it is just a handle, so there is something to click and something for the ruler to reach. It could sit anywhere on the ring, so it is put on the other point's meridian.
l7.d7: The numbers are still exact. Pole to pole is 10,800 nautical miles: 180 degrees at sixty miles to the degree. The straight ruler agrees exactly, because that line is a meridian, and a meridian is a radial.
l7.d8: This also explains the blank ring at the edge of the sheet. Antarctica is not missing because nobody had been there. A continent that wraps around the south pole gets stretched the way the pole does, smeared along the whole rim, at a scale that grows without limit as you get closer.
l7.d9: Switch to Recentred on A and it mirrors. The south pole becomes the centre. The north pole becomes the rim.
l7.d10: No projection escapes this. Mercator does it to both poles at once, stretching each into the full width of the map, top and bottom. That is why Greenland comes out looking the size of Africa on it. Every map projection is a set of choices about where to put the stretching.

about.lead: The sheet turns a difference of longitude into a difference of sun time, and turns that back into a distance. Its own title says so, printed in the corner: Longitude and Time Calculator.
about.p1: The sun moves fifteen degrees of longitude every hour. So one degree is four minutes.
about.p2: If you know when it is noon where you are, and when it is noon somewhere else, the gap between those two moments is an angle. Take that angle and multiply it by sixty and you have the distance in nautical miles. Convert to whatever unit you like from there.
about.h2: The three numbers it runs on
about.p4: Everything else on the sheet is a way of reading those three off the page without arithmetic.
about.p5: The map came with two arms pivoted at the centre. You lay one arm along your own meridian and the other along the place you want. The angle between the arms is the difference of longitude. Read it as time at four minutes to the degree.
about.p6: One arm on Greenwich, the other on New York. The angle between them is about 74 degrees. 74 × 4 = 296 minutes, so four hours and fifty-six minutes. When it is noon in London it is a little after seven in the morning in New York.
about.p7: That reading is exact. It needs no scale and no ruler, only the angle.
about.p8: A difference of longitude is an angle, and an angle becomes a distance only once you know where on the sphere it is measured. A degree of longitude is sixty miles at the equator, thirty at sixty degrees of latitude, and nothing at all at the pole.
about.p9: So for a distance between two places you need the angle between the places, not just the angle between their meridians. The two latitudes give you that. Once you have it, it is sixty miles to the degree as before.
about.p10: That is the calculation the chart page runs, step by step, with your numbers in it.
about.p11: The mile scale along the bottom of the sheet is meant to be used from the centre outward. That is why the arms pivot at the centre.
about.p12: Along any line running straight out from the middle, the scale is exact. That is the one thing this projection guarantees, and it is the only place the guarantee holds. The other scale along the bottom is a longitude and time scale. It is not a general ruler for the picture.
about.p13: Laying a straight edge across the middle of the map and reading the bottom scale off it.
about.p14: That is not what the scale is for, and the answer comes out wrong, sometimes by more than double. Sydney to Santiago reads 13,856 miles that way against a true 6,118.
about.p15: The distance is not set by the picture. It is set by the gridded network of longitude and latitude behind it. The picture is one way of laying that network out flat. Read the network and you get the right answer. Read the picture and you do not.
about.p16: This is an azimuthal equidistant projection. It preserves direction from its centre, and it rectifies great circle arcs measured from that centre into straight lines. A curve on the sphere comes out straight on the paper and still stands for the same distance. That is a feature of the tool.
about.p17: Every flat map is a projection of the same spherical coordinate system, the graticule of latitude and longitude. They differ in where they put the stretching, not in what they are drawing. Discredit one on those grounds and you have discredited all of them, Mercator included.
about.p18: Open the chart, set two places, and read the panel. It shows the longitude, the sun time, the angle and the distance, with the arithmetic written out underneath. The worked examples run through the cases in order, including what happens when you move the centre of the projection to the place you are measuring from.

gallery.lead: The map disc is only the middle of the sheet. Around it Gleason printed the title block, the twenty-four hour dial, two scale rulers, a pair of solstice diagrams and several paragraphs of instruction. These are the copies consulted, reproduced whole. Click any sheet to enlarge it here, and click again to close it.
gallery.note: Shown for what is printed on them, not measured on. Only the reprint on the chart page is georeferenced.
gallery.foot: The 1892 work carries no known copyright restrictions. Each copy is credited to its holding institution above.

ref.quoteNote: Quotations are given in the original English, as they are the primary source. The surrounding text is translated.
ref.foot: Quotations are transcribed from the patent text and from the 1893 printing. Spelling and punctuation are as they appear in the originals.
ref.02: The sheet names its own purpose in the upper left: Longitude and Time Calculator. Patent allowed 15 November 1892.
ref.03: The chart is a circular world map, north pole at the centre, ringed by a dial divided into twenty-four hours in Roman numerals. Around the foot of the dial it prints its own rule: degrees of longitude reduced to sun-time = 4 minutes. Two scale rulers run along the bottom of the sheet, and two small solstice diagrams sit at the lower corners.
ref.05: The chart on this site is a 2013 Lone Star Art reprint held by the American Geographical Society Library, chosen because its map face is clear. The 1892 impression at the Boston Public Library still has an indicating arm pivoted at its centre, lying across Scandinavia and north-west Russia.
ref.06: The 1892 impression, Boston Public Library. The arm is graduated in degrees of latitude and turns about the eyelet at the pole, exactly as the patent specifies. The reprint omits it.
ref.07: The two agree geometrically. Fitted independently, the reprint's scale stands to the original's in the ratio 1.2513, against a sheet-width ratio of 1.2529, so the reprint reproduces the plate to about a tenth of a percent. Both put the Greenwich meridian at 90.0° from image north.
ref.09: Gleason filed on 15 August 1892 and was granted U.S. Patent 497,917 on 23 May 1893. The title on the drawing sheet is Time-Chart.
ref.10: Fig. 1, the circular map with its dial and indicating arms. Figs. 2 and 3 show the pivot at the centre.
ref.12: That sentence fixes the geometry completely. The centre is the north pole, latitude runs outward to 90° South at the rim, and the spacing is even. Combined with the meridians:
ref.13: A map with straight radial meridians holding their true longitude, and evenly spaced latitude circles measured from the centre, is an azimuthal equidistant projection centred on the north pole. That is a standard projection, still used for polar route charts and for the emblem of the United Nations. Its defining property is the one its name states: distances are equidistant, meaning true to scale, along radials from the centre. Along any other line they are not.
ref.14: How it is meant to be worked
ref.15: The instrument is worked by swinging two arms about the centre and reading the angle between them against the hour dial. Every operation the patent describes is an angular one, taken about the pole.

ref.43: Gleason states the mile relation three times and the three do not quite agree: 5280 against 6075 feet gives 1.15057, the 69.16 English miles to the degree gives 1.15267, and Fig. 37’s 208 against 180 gives 1.15556. This replication uses the foot definition, since that is a definition rather than a reading taken off a ruler. The difference is about half a mile in two hundred.
ref.45: The stated outputs are latitude, longitude, and difference of time. Distance between two arbitrary places by straight edge is not among them, and no passage in chapter XVII offers such a method.
ref.46: Reading distance off an azimuthal equidistant chart
ref.47: Three cases, in order of how much work they take.
ref.49: Any line running straight out from the centre is a meridian, and the chart is true to scale along it. Pole to anywhere, or two points on the same meridian, can be measured with a straight edge and read against the latitude scale directly. The chart itself carries this scale on its indicating arm, which is why the arm is graduated in degrees of latitude.
ref.51: A degree of longitude is 60 geographical miles at the equator and shrinks with the cosine of the latitude: 30 miles at 60°, and nothing at the pole. Gleason tabulates this in his Fig. 43, Diagram showing Longitude in Miles at any Latitude North or South of the Equator (p. 402). A degree of longitude is a fixed amount of time everywhere, four minutes, but it is not a fixed distance.
